name: Soul-body dualism
plain_explanation: Plato treats the soul and the body as two fundamentally different things: the soul is akin to the eternal, unchanging Ideas, while the body belongs to the changing, sensible world, and death is simply their separation.
precise_definition: Plato's metaphysical pairing, in the Phaedo, of soul with reality/ideas/reason and body with appearance/sensible-objects/sense-perception, in which the first term of each pair is superior in both reality and goodness to the second, with death defined as the soul's separation from the body.
why_it_mattered: It grounds both Plato's epistemology (the body is a hindrance to true knowledge) and his ethics (the philosopher should minimize attachment to bodily concerns), and was adopted, in modified form, by Christianity.
historical_origin: Traced by Russell to Orphic religious doctrine, in which the soul is 'the child of earth and of the starry heaven,' the body from earth, the soul from heaven.
examples: 'Death is the separation of soul and body.'
objections: Russell notes Christianity adopted the dualism only in part, blocked by two obstacles Plato's logic does not face: that a good Creator could not have made a body-based world if the body is evil, and that orthodox Christianity, unlike the Manichaeans, could never condemn marriage outright.
influence_on_later_thinkers: Became 'a commonplace in philosophy and science and popular thought' as the mind/matter distinction, per Russell, despite its religious origin.
connection_to_politics_or_religion: Rooted in Orphic religious doctrine of the soul's divine origin and the body's earthly origin.
